sender.en: A new online friend or a stranger

name.en: Sextortion: “pay or I’ll share your photos”

how.en: It often starts on social media, a messaging app or a game, with someone who seems to be your age and interested in a relationship, or who offers something of value. Once they have intimate photos or videos, they threaten to send them to your family and friends or post them unless you pay or send more. Sometimes the first message is already a threat, claiming they have images of you. Teens are often targeted; the FBI received more than 75,000 sextortion reports in 2025.

text.en: Someone you met online flirts, or offers you something, and asks for intimate photos.
Once they have them, or say they do, they threaten to send them to your family and friends.
They demand money, gift cards or crypto, or more images, and set a short deadline.
They tell you not to tell anyone, and ask for more even after you pay.
I have your pics and I have a list of all your followers and family. Send $500 in the next hour or I send everything to all of them. Don’t test me.

en: A new online contact who quickly asks for intimate images.
Threats to share images with your contacts unless you pay.
Short deadlines and demands for gift cards, crypto or payment apps.
“Help” services that charge a fee to make it stop.
Don’t pay and don’t send anything more. Stop replying and block them, but keep the messages.
Talk to someone you trust. It’s not your fault.
Report it to the FBI. If the victim is under 18, also report it to the NCMEC CyberTipline.
Ask the platform to remove the images; the law requires them to act within 48 hours of your request.
Be careful with paid services promising to remove images or stop the threats.

sources.title: How to avoid deceptive sextortion assistance services and find real help
